## Author-provided scientific guidance

### Reported working model and formation-selectivity investigation

Mechanistically, the formation of aromatic cyclopropenium cations from the [2 + 1] cycloaddition products under acidic conditions appears to be reasonable (Figure 4A). Cyclopropenium cations are known to be relatively stable intermediates due to their aromaticity and the stabilizing effects of the positive charge delocalized over the ring.<sup>25–30</sup> However, the equilibrium among multiple π-type cyclopropenium cations would pose a significant challenge in achieving selectivity control during subsequent reactions with MeOH. Interestingly, the reaction between 1a and 2a showed excellent regioselectivity and the regioisomer 3a<sup>′</sup> was only obtained in 2% yield, without the observation of regioisomer 3a<sup>′′</sup> (3a, 1.61 g, 82% yield, Figure 4B). In order to understand the origin of regioselectivity of the reaction, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations on the nucleophilic addition step (Figure 4A). Our results indicate that methanol nucleophilic addition to the cyclopropenium cation intermediate occurs preferentially at the carbon atom adjacent to the difluoromethyl group. In the transition state TS-1, a hydrogen bonding is formed between the OH group of methanol and the F atom of the difluoromethyl group. This hydrogen bonding stabilizes the transition state TS-1, resulting in the lowest activation energy. In contrast, the other two transition states TS-1<sup>′</sup> and TS-1<sup>′′</sup> have higher free energy barriers due to steric repulsion between the methyl and phenyl groups (for details, see Figure S9). Label and attachment correspondence, verified from the original structural figures: 1a and 2a are the phenylacetylene and acylsilane in PI1/PI2, the isolated siloxy substrate A is siloxy_start, and 3a, 3a′ and 3a″ are methoxy_major, methoxy_minor and methoxy_comparator, respectively. TS-1 depicts methanol approaching the ring carbon directly bearing CF2H; TS-1′ approaches the hydrogen-bearing ring carbon; TS-1″ approaches the phenyl-bearing ring carbon. This graph-resolved correspondence clarifies the text's phrase adjacent to the difluoromethyl group; the three transition-state depictions use the same phenyl/CF2H-substituted cyclopropenium/methanol model.

### Reported product comparison

Furthermore, we also investigated the stability of the three possible isomers and found that the Gibbs free energy of compound 3a was 3.2 kcal/mol lower than that of 3a<sup>′</sup>, and 7.2 kcal/mol lower than that of 3a<sup>′′</sup>, indicating that compound 3a is the thermodynamically most-stable isomer. This calculation result is consistent to the experimental study that 3a<sup>′</sup> was converted to 3a in 91% yield when 3a<sup>′</sup> was subjected to MeOH in the presence of 5 mol % of TMSCl, indicating the equilibrium of 3a, 3a<sup>′</sup>, and 3a<sup>′′</sup> under the reaction conditions (Figure 4A).

### Reported stability interpretation

We propose that the intermediates 3a and 3a<sup>′</sup> are more stable than 3a″ due to the conjugation between the phenyl group and the C=C bond. The lower stability of 3a<sup>′</sup> compared with 3a might be due to the fact that when an electron-withdrawing group (EWG) is directly attached to the C=C bond, it can decrease the electron density, thereby weakening the strength of the π bond.<sup>24</sup>

### Reported computational protocol

All DFT calculations were performed using the Gaussian 16 series of programs <sup>[s9]</sup>. The M06-2X exchange-correlation functional <sup>[s10]</sup> was used for all DFT calculations, solvent effects of dichloromethane were considered in geometric optimizations with the SMD solvent model <sup>[s11]</sup>, and under this protocol, the structures of the intermediates and transition states were optimized and characterized by frequency analyses using a 6-311+G(d,p) <sup>[s12-s13]</sup> basis set for all atoms. Vibrational frequency calculations were performed for all stationary points to confirm if each optimized structure is a local minimum. All minima (intermediates) have no imaginary frequencies, and all optimized transition state structures have only one imaginary (negative) frequency.

### Original-figure comparison, transcribed from the inspected labels

The inspected transition-state figure labels TS-1, TS-1′ and TS-1″ with ΔΔG‡ = 0.0 kcal/mol, ΔΔG‡ = 1.3 kcal/mol and ΔΔG‡ = 7.1 kcal/mol, respectively. These are relative transition-state Gibbs-energy differences, not absolute barriers. The TS-1 depiction labels the O-H···F hydrogen-bond contact as 2.39 Å and the forming C-O distances as 1.91 Å, 1.94 Å and 1.82 Å for TS-1, TS-1′ and TS-1″, respectively.

### Reporting limits of the supplied baseline

Reporting limits of the supplied baseline (not additional author-performed work): the reported methods specify geometry optimization and frequency characterization but do not specify an IRC protocol, thermochemical temperature or standard-state conventions. The displayed energy differences have no reported numerical uncertainty estimates. The available comparison is methanol-addition competition and relative product stability, not a computed full photochemical/acid-exchange network. Document unspecified details as ambiguities and justify substitutions rather than inventing an unreported author recipe. Experimental reporting discrepancies are not resolved by pretending that the preparations were identical. The gram-scale main overview specifies 12 h illumination, while the detailed SI scheme and procedure specify 24 h; both use DCM at a nominal alkyne concentration of 1.0 M, rather than the small-scale 0.2 M. The minor-interconversion SI prose instead prints 3a as the starting material, a 0.6-equivalent annotation for 0.6 mmol MeOH, and 1.0 mL DCM for 0.2 mmol substrate, and omits TMSCl. The main text and the mutually consistent main/SI interconversion drawings identify the minor 3a′ as the starting material, 3.0 equivalents MeOH, 5 mol% TMSCl and DCM (0.1 M); the shared public endpoint uses those drawings and the main text. Preserve these experimental reporting limitations separately from the mutually consistent computed product and transition-state comparisons. The endpoint is not by itself proof of equilibrium, and a disclosed result is guidance, not evidence that the solver executed a calculation.
